title: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis (leanprover-community.github.io)
comments: While still possible, the proof exploiting a bug is vanishingly small now. Following a few bugs and bad proofs this year, there are a number of different implementations, in different languages, and with different levels of proofs of their consistency. con-leche and con-ron are the heavy hitters, with consistency proofs of themselves. So for RH to be false, there'd have to be a bug in all the kernels that affects both the consistency proofs and the RH proof itself.reply

Since I'm not terribly familiar with Lean, math folks are generally satisfied the provided proof encodes the RH correctly I presume?edit: I need to learn to read, that's the first part of their statement.The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory.reply
The statement of RH that it proves is taken directly from Mathlib, so it's extremely well-vetted and longstanding (from my understanding).reply

Correct.They don't use some random definition of RiemannHypothesis, they use the version here: https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib...Note that this definition is years old. It's very well vetted. It's not a case of "the proof works, it just doesn't actually prove what you think it proves".If you read the blog post, it says they added a "Challenge.lean" file. What that means is that instead of taking for granted the proof is trying to prove Riemann, they added a small file which reads RiemannHypothesis from the Mathlib library mentioned above, and forces the proof to match that.They also mention running comparator, which is important because it checks for all the ways a proof might mathematically "cheat". For example, if you are trying to prove 1+2=5, and you redefine 2 as 4, then your bad proof would actually compile in Lean at first, but then comparator checks would discover all the tricks like that and declare the proof invalid.Additionally, they mention compiling the proof with different Lean kernels, not just the mainline one. This rules out a way a proof This means the proof cannot just take advantage of a bug in the mainline Lean kernel. Importantly, they mention compiling the proof with con-leche, which uses a kernel that has been mathematically verified. Using con-leche is a lot slower, but the fact that the proof works on multiple kernels including con-leche means that it's not taking advantage of some bug in Lean.At this point, I would say the proof is almost certainly true. The only obvious way it could be false is if ZFC itself is inconsistent or something wild like that, and the proof took advantage of it. But if ZFC is inconsistent, all of mathematics is in trouble.reply
why is the verification is so fast this time while last time (a few weeks ago? and I can't remember name of that theorem) it took a few weeks and they finally found an error in Claude's proof?reply

Isn’t Lean stronger than ZFC? I thought you could prove Con(ZFC) within Lean. So it’s possible that the formal system encoded by Lean is inconsistent but ZFC is not. (I don’t consider this that likely, though.)reply

Yes, Lean is stronger than ZFC. But two of the checkers, con=leche and con-ron, don't just verify based on Lean. They come with a formal proof from set theory that they cannot wind up accepting an incorrect proof.In other words you can ignore Lean. We have a proof from ZFC, of the Riemann Hypothesis. We have a proof, acceptable in ZFC, that this proof is correct.In other words Lean's dependent type theory is used to arrange its understanding of the proof. But the actual reasoning that you wind up with for this proof does not need anything that doesn't follow from ZFC.reply
Yes, Lean is stronger than ZFC. lean has been shown to be consistent with ZFC + infinitely many inaccessible cardinals.reply
If ZFC is inconsistent, every well-formed closed formula is s theorem, and thus has a proof.reply

True but irrelevant ... in fact, that's a fallacy of affirmation of the consequent. That every statement can be proven from logical explosion (if ZFC is not consistent) does not mean that every proof is a result of logical explosion.Consider Euclid's proof that there is no greatest prime. It is valid regardless of whether ZFC is consistent.Similarly, the Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis depends on Lean's type theory, not ZFC's consistency. It's an explicit machine-checked proof term, not a non-constructive consequence of logical explosion.reply

title: Inkling-2-Mini in 5.4 GB Memory (github.com/shinmegamiboson)
comments: If you're new to quantized models: Don't get too excited about claims of fitting large models into tiny RAM footprints from random GitHub repos. There is always a tradeoff, and it's too easy to benchmaxx KL-divergence numbers and even single benchmark scores. Just because you can get something to run on a device doesn't mean it's going to be useful. The headline claim of this repo (12X better) doesn't even apply to Inkling-2-MiniThis repo's README is a mess of different histories as the author bounces from one popular model to the next. It refers to vague things like "the 1.2GB file" that probably made sense in an early vibecoding pass, but are now lost after the repo has been pushed around to different popular models.The truth is that random GitHub repos with messy READMEs almost never hold a real secret that the mainstream quantizations have missed. I would recommend sticking to mainstream quantizations like the official GGML release, Unsloth's quants, or the more well known community quantizers like bartowski or AesSedai. They typically follow an optimized size-quality tradeoff so you can find the one that fits your needs.When you see a repo like this where everything is so obviously vibecoded that the README is a rambling mix of projects and claims, you should probably go looking for a more authoritative source. The local LLM communities get spammed with 10 of these types of projects per day but I have yet to see a real breakthrough come from any of the vibecoded ones. The real work is coming from people who study this and have compute to test at scale or work on implementing advanced techniques which require inference engine support, like trellis quants.reply
Yep. Tried GLM-5.3  1 or 2bit (don't remember), it should be something like 80% as good according to the divergence chart, in reality it's dogshit.reply
Yeah, q8_0 is where I prefer to live, q4_0 if absolutely necessary. And quantizing the KV cache is for suckers.reply

> it's too easy to benchmaxx KL-divergence numbersCould you elaborate on this? Intuitively how can the distribution over logits be similar and the results different?reply

KL divergence is computed over samples from a text corpus. WikiText-2 is commonly used, which is a sampling of Wikipedia articles.Quantization processes are somewhat complex and are more involved than uniformly truncating bits. Look up imatrix quants for a sampling of some of the techniques used. The short story is that the quantization is performed in a way that prioritizes weights which matter to a certain corpus. The corpus used as the input to that process therefore biases where the quantization losses go.It's common to use a corpus like WikiText-2 from Wikipedia articles, but you can imagine a random sampling of wikipedia articles may not be favorable to, for example, programming work. A lot of quantizers keep their corpus as a secret sauce, so you may not even be able to see what they're prioritizing or even how some of them measure KL divergence.You can get amazing KL divergence numbers if you basically train the quantization on some text corpus and then measure KL divergence on it.This is also why you can't compare KL divergence numbers from different sources unless you've verified that they're computed in the same way.There are a lot of quants out there that claim amazing KL divergence numbers but are really bad for programming work, for example. If you want to do continuations of Wikipedia articles they might be great.reply
Validation dataset. Nobody shares or talks about their validation dataset v.s. their calibration data when doing this kind of quantization / publishing KLD numbers.reply
yup, this. calibrating on wikitext and then validating on it is a shady movereply
first_paragraph: A quantization compiler that delivers 12× lower KL than Q4_K_M at the same file sizeLookAtMyQuant is a quantization compiler. It measures how much each stored piece of a model hurts the output when compressed. It then picks a code for each piece so the whole model fits a size budget with the least damage.On Gemma 4 E2B, its GGUF has 12× lower KL than Q4_K_M at the same file size. The method and every result are on the site.The code is under the MIT license.LookAtMyQuant 2 takes Qwen3.5-4B to 1.23 GB, 2.3 bits per weight. The file solves 330 of 540 exact-answer math problems. I guess it is if you haven’t worked with this sort of thing beforepcap is a file format for packer captures. You can use tools to capture copies of all packets traversing a network interface, both on clients and servers running operating systems like Linux and Windows, and on network switches and routers that support this (at a minimum, with enterprise gear you can at least send a copy of all traffic from specific source and destination interfaces in both receive and transmit directions to other interfaces you connect a “sniffer” to that you then run a pcap capture on, or you can often even encapsulate the copied traffic in GRE tunnel payloads and send them directly to a remote sniffer).This is a local web app that uses Python libraries to analyze these capture files and look for common tell tale signs of specific issues, such as a TCP connection being opened and being immediately reset, which is an excellent way to find firewalls in the path that are denying connections. You can also, providing an API key, send the capture and analysis result to an LLM to discuss things further.A sufficiently talented network engineer can do this by hand, but can save time with this tool. End users that aren’t capable of interpreting the capture due to lack of knowledge of underlying network protocols can also get results this way without escalation.reply

comments: This reminds me of a (completely different, but felt equally) bizzare problem with ghostty (the terminal emulator) on Linux and Steam, specifically Baldur's Gate 3.At the start of the game after an update, BG3 compiles the (Vulkan) shaders. To avoid hammering the computer, it checks the load, including I/O pressure, and then throttles itself. It turns out that Ghostty uses io_uring, and even if it's not doing anything this somehow counts as pressure. This was made worse by the fact that I usually have a dozen or so Ghostty windows.End result, BG3 compiles shaders using 1 core, throttled, instead of all available 20 cores. Instead of a minute or so, it'd take several hours.(For closure: I configured ghostty to use epoll instead. Probably not optimal but works around the problem.)reply

Interesting to see the "io_uring vs io pressure measurement" issue come up here; it's turned up on qemu-devel recently too: https://lore.kernel.org/qemu-devel/4EF13FE7-E6F3-42E2-83F9-6...If I am reading the thread correctly, the io_uring maintainer's position is that applications trying to use the metric that "poll via io_uring" handles differently from "poll via epoll or select" are fundamentally misguided and measuring something that doesn't make sense, so they don't want to slow down io_uring to placate those apps.reply

From https://lore.kernel.org/qemu-devel/962d44d3-ca7b-4cc8-b0f7-7...> iowait is fundamentally incompatible with sane accounting in the first
place, that is the problem. It really tells you nothing, and was
deprecated since the days of uniprocessor systems. The problem here is
not how iowait is done in the kernel, it's that people are using this
metric in the first place. Which is why you just want to NOT do that,
and do sane accounting on your disk drives, if you care about that kind
of thing.> Which is why I refuse to cater to any kind of iowait accounting metrics,
it's just adding overhead to support a metric that is largely
nonsensical in the first place. It doesn't answer any questions that an
application/tier owner would want to know. Those questions might be
things like "am I I/O bound?" or "is the device I'm using being slow?".
I wish people would realize that, rather than continue to place value in
iowait as a metric for ANYTHING, and stop trying to work around it.It sounds more like their position is "iowait is a useless metric" and that polling with io_uring completely breaks iowait metrics but fixing it would add a minor slowdown so they refuse to do so because they don't think it's a valuable metric to begin with.reply

Status |

Leonida is a static recompilation project. The Xbox Series CPU is x86-64 like a PC, so the game's code is loaded
and run natively, and the console's system software is reimplemented. The console's precompiled RDNA2 GPU programs
are translated to SPIR-V for Vulkan. The game's models, textures and audio are read from your package. All of this
happens on your PC, from your own copy of the game.ImportantThis repository does not contain the game, keys or an executable, and it does not explain how to get them. You
need your own copy, with its files already readable on disk. Nothing here decrypts or works around any protection.
Everything the build creates (the generated shaders, extracted assets, the runtime folder and your saves) comes
from your game and stays on your PC. Never share those files.Discord: https://discord

I keep seeing people rediscovering tried and true software engineering principles and saying AI makes them "matter more"... And I'm a bit skeptical of that framing.Things like platform engineering, DevOps, code quality, linting, CI/CD, QA, etc. were just as foundational before coding agents as they are now (regardless of never being called "pattern engineering"). I'd argue what's changed is less their importance than the consequences of neglecting them.I think a lot of this is how we as an industry are coping with the realization that the narrative we've been sold over the past few years, that AI was going to render software engineering a "solved problem", isn't actually true.So instead of saying "Hm, it looks like being able to arbitrarily generate massive amounts of plausible code has exposed just how much of software engineering was never about writing code in the first place"... We say "Wow, these amazing AI coding agents are so powerful we're having to formalize new levels of abstraction for engaging with software engineering!"Idk, maybe I'm being a yum yucker. People can call stuff whatever they want. Just irks me when there's plenty of prior art, knowledge, instruction, etc. that has run into these problems years and years ago that may be more useful to center than coining new shibboleths.reply

I think the difference is in effective bottlenecks. Previously, the ability actually produce code was a bottleneck just as much as the ability to architect and engineer that code, or to make effective product decisions was. Now, the code production bottleneck has been largely reduced - but those other bottlenecks have not been, bringing them to significantly larger prominence.The reason this matters for baseline processes and patterns is that when the system is not set up for AI to trivially copy good practices, it won't, and that will cost the architect and engineering bottlenecks even more just at a time when they are becoming the most obvious limit on velocity.So, yes, they always mattered for lots of reasons. But the relative impact on velocity, which is at the forefront of everyone's mind right now, has changed.reply
I've had a different experience in my career. The ability to produce code was seldom the bottleneck.reply

Now Ü has built-in unit-testing functionality.
Writing a unit-test is as simple as this:halt is used for handling test failures, but it’s recommended to use some macro (like assert) which is able to print into stderr, what exactly went wrong.Running such tests is possible via simple command test supported now by the Ü build system.fn_test is just a special syntax, which allows defining a unit-test function.
Unit-test functions are almost like regular ones, but there are small differences in the way how they are built.
They get internal encoded names, so that it’s not possible to reference a unit-test (call it manually).
They always have external linkage and unit-test functions defined in imported files get comdat, so that they are deduplicated.
Also unit-test functions are marked with special metadata, so that it’s possible to identify them and process later.What happens later is more interesting.
